subsystems.name: Compute payload
subsystems.role: racks of processors and GPUs running jobs in orbit, either autonomously or on commands from the ground.

subsystems.name: Power system
subsystems.role: generate electricity from sunlight, since there is no grid.

subsystems.name: Thermal control
subsystems.role: reject all waste heat by radiation, because vacuum has no air to carry it away.
parts: heat pipes or pumped fluid loops
surface coatings that emit well in infrared

subsystems.name: Communications
subsystems.role: move data in and results out.

subsystems.name: Spacecraft bus
subsystems.role: hold everything in the right attitude and keep the orbit stable.

subsystems.name: Ground segment
subsystems.role: schedule jobs, collect results, and keep the spacecraft healthy.

buildSteps.title: Choose an orbit
buildSteps.detail: A dawn-dusk Sun-synchronous orbit keeps the craft in near-continuous sunlight and holds the radiators permanently facing away from the Sun, which is what makes the physics work.

buildSteps.title: Size the power and thermal systems together
buildSteps.detail: Sunlight at Earth is about 1,360 W/m²; at realistic array efficiency and packing, tens of kilowatts means hundreds of square metres of solar panel. Each kilowatt of that power becomes waste heat that must be radiated: at a few hundred kelvin a radiator emits roughly 400 W per square metre of surface, so radiator area ends up comparable to array area.

buildSteps.title: Select and harden the electronics
buildSteps.detail: Low Earth orbit sits below the worst radiation belts, but cosmic rays and the South Atlantic Anomaly still cause single-event upsets. Parts are chosen for tolerance, shielded where mass allows, and paired with error-correcting memory, watchdogs and periodic reboots.

buildSteps.title: Build the spacecraft bus
buildSteps.detail: Structure, attitude control, batteries and optical terminals are integrated and tested separately from the compute payload.

buildSteps.title: Integrate the racks
buildSteps.detail: Servers are mounted with vibration isolation, wired for power and data, and their heat is coupled into the fluid loop that feeds the radiators.

buildSteps.title: Test on the ground
buildSteps.detail: Thermal-vacuum chambers reproduce the vacuum and temperature swings, shake tables reproduce launch loads, and the whole system is run end-to-end against a ground station.

buildSteps.title: Launch and commission
buildSteps.detail: The craft rideshares to orbit, deploys its arrays and radiators, and is checked out for weeks before taking real work.

buildSteps.title: Operate and dispose
buildSteps.detail: Jobs are scheduled around downlink windows, software is updated in flight, and the satellite is deorbited or moved to a graveyard orbit at end of life rather than left as debris.

prerequisites.why: commercial processors and GPUs fly today in experimental payloads, but error rates rise sharply with performance and time in orbit.
laser terminals have demonstrated hundreds of gigabits per second from small satellites; the bottleneck becomes the number and location of ground stations.

prerequisites.tech: Deployable radiators and two-phase cooling loops
prerequisites.why: these are proven on crewed stations and large satellites, but scaling them into the hundreds of kilowatts a serious data centre would need is unproven.

prerequisites.tech: Cheap, frequent launch to low Earth orbit
prerequisites.why: without low launch cost, the mass of radiators and solar arrays for each kilowatt of compute is prohibitive.
with only intermittent ground contact, the payload must manage failures and workloads without a human in the loop.

pathway.milestone: GPU payloads flown on small satellites, with results returned to ground stations
pathway.unlocks: proof that off-the-shelf compute can survive launch and run in orbit.

pathway.milestone: dedicated compute satellites of tens of kilowatts with laser crosslinks
pathway.unlocks: useful niches where the data is already in orbit — processing Earth-observation imagery before downlinking it instead of sending the raw pixels.

pathway.milestone: clusters of compute satellites sharing work over an inter-satellite mesh
pathway.unlocks: redundancy and the ability to run larger models than one spacecraft can host.

pathway.milestone: orbital capacity large enough to compete with terrestrial data centres on cost per job
pathway.unlocks: a genuine option for compute in regions where land, water or grid connection are the binding constraint — if launch and radiator mass fall far enough.
